Chapter 4: Designing Checklists That Actually Work
You know, not every checklist is created equal. The difference between a checklist that actually helps and one that just slows you down? It’s all in the design. A great checklist isn’t just a list of boxes to tick—it’s a tool that fits right into your workflow, guiding you along without getting in your way.
So, what makes a checklist truly effective? Let’s start with simplicity. The best checklists focus on the critical steps—the ones that could easily get overlooked, but would have serious consequences if forgotten. If you try to include everything, you risk overwhelming people. That’s when “checklist fatigue” kicks in, and folks start ignoring the checklist altogether.
When you’re building a checklist, it helps to think like an editor. Ask yourself: What absolutely has to happen every single time? And what’s so basic, it can be left off the list? The trick is to find a balance—thorough enough to cover what matters, but not so detailed that it becomes a burden.
There are a couple of main types of checklists you’ll come across. First, there’s the do-confirm checklist. Here, you do the task from memory, then pause to double-check the list and make sure nothing slipped through the cracks. Then there’s the read-do checklist—where you actually read each step out loud and do it, checking each item as you go.
Which one should you use? Well, it depends. If you’re working in a fast-paced environment and know the process well, a do-confirm checklist might be just right. But if the task is more complicated or unfamiliar, a read-do approach gives you that extra bit of security.
Timing is also key. The best checklists are built into natural pause points in your routine—those moments where it makes sense to stop and run through a quick review. Think about surgery: checklists happen before anesthesia, before the first incision, and before the patient leaves the operating room. Pilots use them before takeoff, before landing, and in an emergency.
Now, let’s talk about language. A checklist should be crystal clear—simple words, no jargon, nothing that could trip someone up in the heat of the moment. Everything should be easy to read at a glance, with each item grouped logically and in a consistent format.
But even the best draft needs real-world testing. A checklist isn’t finished the moment you write it; it needs to be put to work, refined, and improved based on feedback. Encourage your team to speak up—add missing steps, tweak confusing language, or cut out what’s not needed. The goal is to have a tool people actually want to use, not something they dread.
And here’s something really important—great checklists bring people together. Many include steps where team members introduce themselves, review the plan as a group, or confirm everyone’s role. These little moments? They build trust, boost communication, and make sure everyone’s on the same page.
So, what makes a checklist work? Let’s recap:
It’s short and focused on the essentials. It’s easy to read and use, even when the pressure’s on. It’s woven into the natural flow of your work. It’s always open to feedback and improvement. And, maybe most importantly, it helps the whole team communicate and work together.
When you get these principles right, checklists become more than just paperwork—they’re powerful allies in reducing mistakes and making sure your team delivers consistent, high-quality results, even when things get tough.
